Find R equivalents of Stata commands

Source: R/findit.R, R/findit-tools.R
findit.Rd

Look up Stata commands and their R equivalents in tidystata and other packages.

  • findit(): Search by Stata command, R function, keyword or plain-language question. Omit the query to browse all entries.

  • findit_selection(): Look up highlighted Stata text in the source editor.

  • findit_clip(): Look up Stata text copied to the clipboard.

Usage

findit(command = NULL, ...)

findit_selection()

findit_clip()

Arguments

command

A Stata command, R function, or search phrase. Supply a bare name (findit(reg), findit(left_join)) or a quoted string for full syntax (findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")). R function names may include () or a namespace prefix. Use !!cmd to look up a string stored in cmd. Stata text can also be enclosed in backticks, as in findit(`tab sex region`, row). Recognized variable names and options customize matching examples. Defaults to NULL (all entries).

...

Optional variable names or command hints, captured without evaluation. Names customize examples in Stata operand order, while hints prioritize examples (findit(tab, gen)). Hints accept exact or unambiguous prefixes of at least three letters. Quote names that conflict with hints (findit(tab, "gen")). Use !! for stored strings. Only unnamed names and strings are accepted.

Value

A tibble of class tidystata_findit with one row per matching Stata idiom and five columns: match (match type), stata (Stata code), r (equivalent R code), package (primary R package), and task (description). The returned object contains every selected match, including any hidden by printing. If nothing matches, a zero-row result with the same columns and class is returned invisibly with an explanatory message. findit_selection() and findit_clip() print the result once and return it invisibly.

Details

Choosing a match

Bare Stata commands return their whole command family. A specific query returns one preferred answer when the match is clear, or up to ten relevant candidates when ambiguous. An omitted query returns the full reference.

Stata abbreviations (reg, regr, regress) are accepted; R functions need their full names. Exact-case matches take priority. Shared names such as log include both interpretations, with Stata matches first. When neither matches, lookup searches keywords. Plain-language questions use curated English and Chinese keywords and synonyms.

Syntax and hints refine the ranking; by and bysort favor grouped operations. Within the same operation, tidystata examples come first, followed by tidyverse, then other packages or base R. Supplied variable names customize compatible examples. Unfamiliar syntax keeps generic examples; notes explain unresolved placeholders or unsupported combinations.

Reading the result

Results print as Stata/R code pairs: one clear match or up to five representative examples. Use print(n = Inf) to show every returned match. Footers distinguish hidden candidates from broader command-family examples and indicate when the ten-candidate limit applies. Specific queries exclude unrelated family entries.

Printing omits package labels and unnecessary prefixes for R's default packages, but keeps ambiguous names such as stats::filter() qualified. Returned code and package metadata are unchanged. The match column records "stata", "r", "keyword", "nearest" or "all".

Editor and clipboard

Select or copy one nonempty Stata command. findit_selection() also runs through the Find Stata equivalent addin; it needs rstudioapi and a source-selection API, as in RStudio or a compatible Positron session. findit_clip() needs clipr and access to a text clipboard. Both preserve the original text and print the lookup result without executing any code.

Text input and language

Quote multiword syntax, reserved words ("if") and non-R names ("_n"). Backticks accept the same Stata text as strings, preserving internal quotes. If the Stata text itself contains backticks, use an R string or raw string.

Lookup works offline; external packages are needed only to run their examples. Descriptions follow R's language settings; Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en") switches Chinese descriptions to English. This curated reference does not parse or execute arbitrary Stata programs. See the "Coming from Stata" articles for guidance.

Examples

findit(reg)
#> # Linear regression
#> Stata: regress y x1 x2
#> R:     fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data)
#> # Note: summary(fit) shows the coefficient table; broom::tidy(fit) returns it as a data frame.
#> 
#> # Fit linear regression through the origin
#> Stata: regress y x z, noconstant
#> R:     lm(y ~ x + z - 1, data=data)
#> # Note: OLS coefficient correspondence requires the same complete-case sample, contrasts and weights. R returns an lm object; Stata coefficient tables and stored estimates have a different structure.
#> 
#> # Include two continuous main effects and their interaction
#> Stata: regress y c.x##c.z
#> R:     lm(y ~ x * z, data=data)
#> # Note: OLS coefficient correspondence requires the same complete-case sample, contrasts and weights. R returns an lm object; Stata coefficient tables and stored estimates have a different structure.
#> 
#> # Fit a quadratic regression
#> Stata: regress y c.x##c.x
#> R:     lm(y ~ x + I(x^2), data=data)
#> # Note: OLS coefficient correspondence requires the same complete-case sample, contrasts and weights. R returns an lm object; Stata coefficient tables and stored estimates have a different structure.
#> 
#> # Adjust regression for a categorical predictor
#> Stata: regress y i.g c.x
#> R:     lm(y ~ factor(g) + x, data=data)
#> # Note: OLS coefficient correspondence requires the same complete-case sample, contrasts and weights. R returns an lm object; Stata coefficient tables and stored estimates have a different structure.
#> 
#> # 13 more relevant examples. To see them all: findit(reg) |> print(n = Inf)

findit(tab, gen)
#> # Dummy variables for every category [tidystata]
#> Stata: tabulate x, generate(x_)
#> R:     as_dummy(data, x)
#> # Note: as_dummy(data, x, .names = "index") numbers the columns x_1, x_2, ... as Stata does. Also: fastDummies::dummy_cols(data, "x"). as_dummy() defaults to value-based column names; .names = "index" gives numbered Stata-style suffixes. Check the missing-category indicator policy too.
#> 
#> # 1 more relevant example. To see them all: findit(tab, gen) |> print(n = Inf)
#> # 26 broader tabulate examples. Browse the family: findit(tabulate)

findit(tab, sex, region)
#> # Two-way cross-tabulation [tidystata]
#> Stata: tabulate sex region
#> R:     tab2(data, sex, region)
#> # Note: fre2(data, x1, x2) adds row and column totals. tidystata retains missing categories by default; Stata tabulate excludes them unless missing is specified. Use .missing = FALSE to match Stata. tab2() and fre2() need explicit .by for grouped tables; inherited grouping columns otherwise remain ordinary variables. fre2() displays row value labels, while column headers retain category codes.
#> 
#> # 9 more relevant examples. To see them all: findit(tab, sex, region) |> print(n = Inf)
#> # Only the 10 best candidates are retained; refine the query for a closer match.
#> # 8 broader tabulate examples. Browse the family: findit(tabulate)

findit(`tab sex region`, row)
#> # Compute percentages within each table row [dplyr]
#> Stata: tabulate sex region, row
#> R:     dplyr::mutate(dplyr::count(data, sex, region), percent = 100 * n / sum(n), .by = sex)
#> # Note: Returns one row per observed combination; empty cells are omitted.
#> 
#> # 26 broader tabulate examples. Browse the family: findit(tabulate)

findit("tab sex region, row")
#> # Compute percentages within each table row [dplyr]
#> Stata: tabulate sex region, row
#> R:     dplyr::mutate(dplyr::count(data, sex, region), percent = 100 * n / sum(n), .by = sex)
#> # Note: Returns one row per observed combination; empty cells are omitted.
#> 
#> # 26 broader tabulate examples. Browse the family: findit(tabulate)

findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
#> # Keep matched rows only [dplyr]
#> Stata: merge 1:1 id using data2, keep(match)
#> R:     inner_join(data1, data2, by = "id")
#> # Note: dplyr retains overlapping non-key columns with suffixes instead of Stata master values, creates no _merge, and does not enforce a declared 1:1 key constraint.
#> 
#> # merge(): Merge two data frames (base R)
#>   Related Stata: merge
#> 
#> # 12 broader merge examples. Browse the family: findit(merge)
#> 
#> # This syntax could not be customized; examples retain generic placeholders.

findit("how do I remove duplicate rows")
#> # Closest entries for "how do I remove duplicate rows"
#> 
#> # Drop rows that duplicate an earlier row [tidystata]
#> Stata: duplicates drop
#> R:     duplicates_drop(data)
#> 
#> # 9 more relevant examples. To see them all: findit("how do I remove duplicate rows") |> print(n = Inf)
#> # Only the 10 best candidates are retained; refine the query for a closer match.

findit(left_join)
#> # Keep all rows of the master data [dplyr]
#> Stata: merge 1:1 id using data2, keep(master match)
#> R:     left_join(data1, data2, by = "id")
#> # Note: dplyr retains overlapping non-key columns with suffixes instead of Stata master values, creates no _merge, and does not enforce a declared 1:1 key constraint.
#> 
#> # 3 more relevant examples. To see them all: findit(left_join) |> print(n = Inf)

# Filter the complete reference
entries <- findit()
entries |>
  dplyr::filter(package == "tidystata")
#> # Find the R equivalent of a Stata command [tidystata]
#> Stata: findit command
#> R:     findit(command)
#> # Note: Bare words and comma-separated names work: findit(tab, sex, region). Add hints such as findit(tab, gen), or quote full Stata syntax. A bare command browses its whole family and shows up to five operations; a clear specific query returns one answer, and ambiguous queries retain up to ten relevant candidates. print(n = Inf) expands the returned results; use the bare command for broader family operations. Within a matching operation, recommendations prefer tidystata, then tidyverse, then other packages or base R. findit() with no argument returns the whole catalogue.
#> 
#> # 143 more relevant examples. To see them all: findit() |> print(n = Inf)

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Highlight tab sex region, row in the source editor, then run:
findit_selection()

# Copy tab sex region, row to the clipboard, then run:
findit_clip()
} # }
